5.1: In the morning, when you get up unwillingly, let this thought be present: I am rising to do the work of a human being. Why then am I dissatisfied, if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world? Or was I made for this, to lie under the bedclothes and keep myself warm?—But this is more pleasant.—Do you exist, then, to take your pleasure, and not at all for action or effort? Don't you see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees, working together to put in order their several parts of the universe? And are you unwilling to do the work of a human being, and do you not hurry to do what is according to your nature?—But it is necessary to rest too.—It is necessary. However, Nature has set limits to this too: she has set limits to eating and drinking, and yet you go beyond these limits, beyond what is enough; yet in your actions it is not so, but you stop short of what you can do. So you do not love yourself, for if you did, you would love your nature and her will. But those who love their various crafts wear themselves out working at them unwashed and without food; but you value your own nature less than the turner values the art of turning, or the dancer the art of dancing, or the lover of money his money, or the vain man his little bit of glory. And such men, when they are passionately devoted to a thing, choose neither to eat nor to sleep rather than to perfect the things they care about. But are the acts which concern society more worthless in your eyes, and less worthy of your effort?
5.2: How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troublesome or unsuitable, and immediately to be in complete tranquillity.
5.3: Judge every word and deed that is according to nature to be fit for you; and do not be turned aside by the blame that follows from anyone, nor by their words, but if a thing is good to be done or said, do not consider it unworthy of you. For those people have their own leading principle and follow their own impulse; pay no attention to these things, but go straight on, following your own nature and the common nature; and the way of both is one.
5.4: I go on through the things that happen according to nature until I fall and rest, breathing out my breath into that element from which I draw it in every day, and falling upon that earth from which my father gathered the seed, and my mother the blood, and my nurse the milk; from which for so many years I have been supplied with food and drink; which bears me when I tread on it and misuse it for so many purposes.
5.5: You say: Men cannot admire the sharpness of your wits.—So be it: but there are many other things of which you cannot say, I am not formed for them by nature. Show those qualities, then, which are entirely in your power: sincerity, seriousness, endurance of hard work, aversion to pleasure, contentment with your lot and with few things, kindness, frankness, no love of excess, freedom from triviality, magnanimity. Don't you see how many qualities you are able to show straight away, in which there is no excuse of natural inability and unfitness, and yet you still choose to remain below the mark? Or are you compelled, through being poorly equipped by nature, to grumble, and to be stingy, and to flatter, and to find fault with your poor body, and to try to please men, and to make a great show, and to be so restless in your mind? No, by the gods; you could have been freed from these things long ago. Only, if in truth you can be charged with being rather slow and dull of understanding, you must make an effort about this too, not neglecting it nor yet taking pleasure in your dullness.
5.6: One man, when he has done a service to another, is ready to set it down to his account as a favour given. Another is not ready to do this, but still in his own mind he thinks of the man as his debtor, and he knows what he has done. A third, in a way, does not even know what he has done, but is like a vine which has produced grapes, and seeks nothing more once it has produced its proper fruit. As a horse when it has run, a dog when it has hunted down the game, a bee when it has made the honey, so a man when he has done a good act does not call out for others to come and see, but goes on to another act, as a vine goes on to produce grapes again in season.—Must a man, then, be one of these, who in a way act like this without noticing it?—Yes.—But this very thing is necessary, noticing what a man is doing: for, it may be said, it is characteristic of the social animal to perceive that he is working in a social way, and indeed to wish that his social partner should perceive it too.—What you say is true, but you do not rightly understand what is now being said: and for this reason you will become one of those I spoke of before, for even they are misled by a certain show of reason. But if you choose to understand the meaning of what is said, do not fear that for this reason you will neglect any social act.
5.7: A prayer of the Athenians: Rain, rain, O dear Zeus, down on the ploughed fields of the Athenians and on the plains.—In truth we ought not to pray at all, or we ought to pray in this simple and noble way.
5.8: Just as we understand what is meant when it is said that Aesculapius prescribed to this man horse-riding, or bathing in cold water, or going without shoes, so we must understand it when it is said that the nature of the universe prescribed to this man disease, or mutilation, or loss, or anything else of the kind. For in the first case "prescribed" means something like this: he prescribed this for this man as something suited to bring about health; and in the second case it means that what happens to, or suits, every man is fixed for him in a way that fits his destiny. For this is what we mean when we say that things suit us, as the workmen say of squared stones in walls or in the pyramids that they suit, when they fit them to one another in some kind of connection. For there is altogether one fitness, one harmony. And as the universe is made up out of all bodies to be such a body as it is, so out of all existing causes necessity, or destiny, is made up to be such a cause as it is. And even those who are completely ignorant understand what I mean; for they say, Destiny brought this to such a person.—This, then, was brought, and this was prescribed to him. Let us then accept these things, as well as those which Aesculapius prescribes. Many of his prescriptions too, as a matter of course, are unpleasant, but we accept them in the hope of health. Let the perfecting and accomplishing of the things which the common nature judges to be good be judged by you to be of the same kind as your health. And so accept everything that happens, even if it seems unpleasant, because it leads to this: to the health of the universe, and to the prosperity and happiness of Zeus, that is, of the universe. For he would not have brought on any man what he has brought, if it were not useful for the whole. Nor does the nature of anything, whatever it may be, cause anything which is not suitable to what is directed by it. For two reasons, then, it is right to be content with what happens to you: the one, because it was done for you and prescribed for you, and in a way had reference to you, spun together with your destiny from the beginning out of the most ancient causes; and the other, because even what comes to each man individually is, to the power which governs the universe, a cause of its happiness and perfection, and indeed of its very continuance. For the integrity of the whole is mutilated if you cut off anything whatever from the connection and continuity either of the parts or of the causes. And you do cut something off, as far as it is in your power, when you are dissatisfied, and in a way try to put something out of the way.
5.9: Do not be disgusted, or discouraged, or dissatisfied, if you do not succeed in doing everything according to right principles; but when you have failed, come back again, and be content if the greater part of what you do is consistent with man's nature, and love what you return to; and do not return to philosophy as if she were a schoolmaster, but act like those who have sore eyes and apply a bit of sponge and egg, or as another applies a plaster, or a soaking with water. For in this way you will not fail to obey reason, and you will rest in it. And remember that philosophy requires only the things your nature requires; but you would have something else, which is not according to nature.—It may be objected: Why, what is more pleasant than this thing I am doing? But is not this the very reason why pleasure deceives us? And consider whether magnanimity, freedom, simplicity, equanimity, piety, are not more pleasant. For what is more pleasant than wisdom itself, when you think of the security and the happy course of all things which depend on the faculty of understanding and knowledge?
5.10: Things are so wrapped up that they have seemed to philosophers, and not a few of them nor ordinary ones, altogether beyond understanding; indeed, even to the Stoics themselves they seem difficult to understand. And all our assent is changeable; for where is the man who never changes? Turn your thoughts, then, to the objects themselves, and consider how short-lived and worthless they are, and that they may be in the possession of a filthy wretch or a whore or a robber. Then turn to the characters of those who live with you, and it is hardly possible to put up with even the most pleasant of them, to say nothing of a man's being hardly able to put up with himself. In such darkness and dirt, then, and in so constant a flux both of substance and of time, and of motion and of things moved, what there is that is worth being highly prized, or even seriously pursued, I cannot imagine. But on the contrary it is a man's duty to comfort himself, and to wait for the natural dissolution, and not to be irritated at the delay, but to rest in these principles only: the one, that nothing will happen to me which is not in keeping with the nature of the universe; and the other, that it is in my power never to act against my god and the spirit within me: for there is no man who will force me to this.
5.11: What am I now using my own soul for? On every occasion I must ask myself this question, and inquire: What do I now have in this part of me which they call the ruling principle? And whose soul do I now have—that of a child, or of a young man, or of a feeble woman, or of a tyrant, or of a domestic animal, or of a wild beast?
5.12: What kind of things those are which seem good to the many, we may learn even from this. For if any man should think of certain things as being really good, such as prudence, temperance, justice, courage, he would not, having first thought of these, bear to listen to anything which was not in harmony with what is really good. But if a man has first thought of as good the things which seem good to the many, he will listen to, and readily accept as very apt, what was said by the comic writer. So even the many perceive the difference. For if it were not so, this saying would not offend and would not be rejected in the first case, while we accept it, when it is said of wealth and of the means that further luxury and fame, as said fittingly and wittily. Go on, then, and ask whether we should value and think good those things to which, once they are first thought of in the mind, the words of the comic writer might aptly be applied—that he who has them, through sheer abundance, has no place to relieve himself in.
5.13: I am made up of the formal and the material; and neither of them will perish into non-existence, just as neither of them came into existence out of non-existence. Every part of me, then, will be changed into some part of the universe, and that again will change into another part of the universe, and so on for ever. And as a consequence of such change I too exist, and those who gave me life, and so on for ever in the other direction. For nothing prevents us from saying so, even if the universe is governed according to fixed periods of revolution.
5.14: Reason and the art of reasoning, that is, philosophy, are powers which are sufficient for themselves and for their own works. They move, then, from a first principle which is their own, and they make their way to the end set before them; and this is why such acts are called Catorthoseis, or right acts, a word which signifies that they proceed by the right road.
5.15: None of these things ought to be called a man's which do not belong to a man as a man. They are not required of a man, nor does man's nature promise them, nor are they the means by which man's nature reaches its end. So neither does the end of man lie in these things, nor yet what helps towards the accomplishment of this end; and what helps towards this end is what is good. Besides, if any of these things did belong to man, it would not be right for a man to despise them and set himself against them; nor would a man deserve praise who showed that he did not want these things, nor would he who denied himself any of them be good, if indeed these things were good. But as it is, the more of these things, or of other things like them, a man deprives himself of, or the more patiently he bears being deprived of any of them, the better a man he is, in just the same degree.
5.16: As your habitual thoughts are, so too will be the character of your mind; for the soul is dyed by its thoughts. Dye it, then, with a continuous series of thoughts such as these: for instance, that where a man can live, there he can also live well. But he must live in a palace; well then, he can also live well in a palace. And again, consider that whatever purpose each thing has been made for, it has been made for this, and it is carried towards this; and its end lies in that towards which it is carried; and where the end is, there too is the advantage and the good of each thing. Now the good for the rational animal is society; for it has been shown above that we are made for society. Is it not plain that the inferior exists for the sake of the superior? But things which have life are superior to those which do not, and of those which have life the superior are those which have reason.
5.17: To seek what is impossible is madness: and it is impossible that the bad should not do something of this kind.
5.18: Nothing happens to any man which he is not formed by nature to bear. The same things happen to another, and either because he does not see that they have happened, or because he wants to show a great spirit, he stands firm and remains unharmed. It is a shame, then, that ignorance and conceit should be stronger than wisdom.
5.19: Things themselves do not touch the soul, not in the least; nor do they have any entry to the soul, nor can they turn or move the soul: but the soul turns and moves itself alone, and whatever judgements it sees fit to make, such it makes for itself the things which present themselves to it.
5.20: In one respect man is the nearest thing to me, so far as I must do good to men and put up with them. But so far as some men make themselves obstacles to my proper acts, man becomes to me one of the things which are indifferent, no less than the sun or the wind or a wild beast. Now it is true that these may impede my action, but they are no impediment to my feelings and disposition, which have the power of acting conditionally and of changing: for the mind converts and changes every hindrance to its activity into an aid; and so what is a hindrance is made to further an act; and what is an obstacle on the road helps us along this road.
5.21: Revere what is best in the universe; and this is what makes use of all things and directs all things. And in the same way also revere what is best in yourself; and this is of the same kind as that. For in you too, what makes use of everything else is this, and your life is directed by this.
5.22: What does no harm to the state does no harm to the citizen. Whenever there seems to be harm, apply this rule: if the state is not harmed by this, neither am I harmed. But if the state is harmed, you must not be angry with the one who harms the state. Show him where his error is.
5.23: Often think of how quickly things pass by and disappear, both the things that are and the things that are coming into being. For substance is like a river in continual flow, and the activities of things are in constant change, and causes work in endless variety; and there is hardly anything which stands still. And consider this which is near you, this boundless abyss of the past and of the future in which all things disappear. How then is he not a fool who is puffed up by such things, or tormented by them, and makes himself miserable? For they trouble him only for a time, and a short time.
5.24: Think of the universal substance, of which you have a very small portion; and of universal time, of which a short and indivisible interval has been assigned to you; and of what is fixed by destiny, and how small a part of it you are.
5.25: Does another do me wrong? Let him see to it. He has his own disposition, his own activity. I now have what the universal nature now wills me to have; and I do what my nature now wills me to do.
5.26: Let the part of your soul which leads and governs be undisturbed by the movements in the flesh, whether of pleasure or of pain; and let it not unite with them, but let it mark out its own bounds and confine those feelings to their own parts. But when these feelings rise up to the mind by virtue of that other sympathy which naturally exists in a body that is all one, then you must not try to resist the sensation, for it is natural; but do not let the ruling part add of itself to the sensation the opinion that it is either good or bad.
5.27: Live with the gods. And he does live with the gods who constantly shows them that his own soul is satisfied with what is assigned to him, and that it does all that the spirit within wishes, which Zeus has given to every man as his guardian and guide, a portion of himself. And this is every man's understanding and reason.
5.28: Are you angry with the man whose armpits stink? Are you angry with the man whose mouth smells foul? What good will this anger do you? He has such a mouth, he has such armpits: such an odour must necessarily come from such things: but the man has reason, it will be said, and he is able, if he takes the trouble, to discover how he gives offence; congratulations on your discovery. Well then, you have reason too: by your rational faculty stir up his rational faculty; show him his error, warn him. For if he listens, you will cure him, and there is no need for anger. Neither tragic actor nor whore.
5.29: As you intend to live when you have gone out,... so it is in your power to live here. But if men do not allow you, then leave life, yet as if you were suffering no harm. The house is smoky, and I leave it. Why do you think this is any trouble? But so long as nothing of the kind drives me out, I remain, am free, and no one shall stop me from doing what I choose; and I choose to do what is according to the nature of the rational and social animal.
5.30: The intelligence of the universe is social. Accordingly it has made the inferior things for the sake of the superior, and it has fitted the superior to one another. You see how it has subordinated, coordinated, and assigned to everything its proper portion, and has brought into harmony with one another the things which are best.
5.31:
How have you behaved up to now towards the gods, your parents, brothers, children, teachers, those who looked after you in infancy, your friends, relatives, your slaves? Consider whether you have so far behaved to all in such a way that this may be said of you:—

“Never has wronged a man in deed or word.”

And call to mind both how many things you have been through, and how many things you have been able to endure, and that the story of your life is now complete and your service is ended; and how many beautiful things you have seen; and how many pleasures and pains you have despised; and how many things called honourable you have spurned; and to how many ill-natured people you have shown kindness.
5.32: Why do unskilled and ignorant souls disturb the one who has skill and knowledge? What soul, then, has skill and knowledge? The one which knows beginning and end, and knows the reason which pervades all substance and which, through all time, by fixed periods or revolutions, governs the universe.
5.33:
Soon, very soon, you will be ashes, or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; but a name is sound and echo. And the things which are much valued in life are empty and rotten and trivial, like little dogs biting one another, and little children quarrelling, laughing, and then straight away crying. But faithfulness and modesty and justice and truth have fled

Up to Olympus from the wide-spread earth.
Hesiod, Works and Days, v. 197.

What then is there that still keeps you here, if the objects of sense are easily changed and never stand still, and the organs of perception are dull and easily receive false impressions, and the poor soul itself is a vapour rising from blood? But to have a good reputation in such a world as this is an empty thing. Why then do you not wait calmly for your end, whether it is extinction or removal to another state? And until that time comes, what is enough? Why, what else but to worship the gods and bless them, and to do good to men, and to practise tolerance and self-restraint; but as to everything which is beyond the limits of the poor flesh and breath, to remember that this is neither yours nor in your power.
5.34: You can pass your life in a steady flow of happiness, if you can go by the right way, and think and act in the right way. These two things are common both to the soul of God and to the soul of man, and to the soul of every rational being: not to be hindered by another; and to hold that good consists in the disposition to justice and the practice of it, and in this to let your desire find its end.
5.35: If this is neither my own badness, nor an effect of my own badness, and the common good is not harmed, why am I troubled about it, and what is the harm to the common good?
5.36:
Do not be carried along thoughtlessly by the appearance of things, but give help to all according to your ability and their fitness; and if they have suffered loss in matters which are indifferent, do not imagine this to be a harm; for it is a bad habit. But as the old man, when he went away, asked for his foster-child's top back, remembering that it was a top, so you too should do in this case.

When you are calling out on the Rostra, have you forgotten, man, what these things are?—Yes; but they are objects of great concern to these people.—Will you too, then, be made a fool for these things? I was once a fortunate man, but I lost it, I don't know how.—But fortunate means that a man has assigned to himself a good fortune: and a good fortune is a good disposition of the soul, good emotions, good actions.
